# The playbook — how we run a website project

The internal guide. Read this before your first project, and hand it to
anyone you bring in. It covers what happens, in what order, who does what, and
the handful of mistakes that cost real money.

Everything referenced here lives in this folder.

---

## The shape of a project

```
ENQUIRY → CALL → PROPOSAL → SIGNED → KICKOFF → REQUIREMENTS → BUILD
   → ROUND 1 → ROUND 2 → LAUNCH → HANDOVER → CARE PLAN
```

Seven of those twelve steps are paperwork. That ratio is correct. The build is
the easy part; everything that goes wrong on a website project goes wrong in
the gaps between the steps.

---

## Stage 1 — Enquiry (same day)

**Goal:** get a call booked, and disqualify early.

Reply within a few hours using script 1 in [email scripts](email-scripts.md).
Don't quote a price. Don't ask what they want built — ask what's not working
now. Send a booking link.

**Disqualify fast when:** the budget is under half the tier's floor and won't
move, they want "just a quick site" with fourteen pages of content they
haven't written, they have three decision-makers who disagree, or they lead
with "should be simple for you". None of these improve. Say no warmly and
recommend someone else; a bad project costs more than an empty week.

---

## Stage 2 — The call (45 min)

**Goal:** understand the business, agree a budget range, know who decides.

Run [the questionnaire](sales-call-questionnaire.md) top to bottom. Two thirds
listening. The three questions that matter most:

1. *What has to be true in twelve months for this to have been worth it?*
2. *Who else has to say yes?*
3. *What's the budget range?* — ask it plainly. If they won't answer, offer
   brackets: "most projects like this land between $5k and $15k — does that
   sound like the right neighbourhood?"

Never quote on the call. "I'll put something together and have it to you
Thursday" buys you the time to price properly and costs you nothing.

---

## Stage 3 — Proposal (within 48h)

Write the [discovery brief](discovery-brief.md) first, for yourself. Then the
[proposal](proposal-template.md), priced from the [rate card](rate-card.md).

**Always offer three options.** Not one. Three prices anchored around the one
you expect them to take makes the decision "which" rather than "whether", and
some clients pick the expensive one for reasons that have nothing to do with
you.

Proposals expire in 14 days. Say so. It's the only polite deadline you get.

---

## Stage 4 — Signed and paid (before anything else)

Contract + deposit, in that order, no exceptions. 50% up front on projects
under $15k; 40/30/30 above.

The temptation to start "while the paperwork catches up" is strongest with the
clients you'll most regret. Starting unpaid teaches them that your timelines
are soft, on day one.

---

## Stage 5 — Kickoff and requirements (week 1)

Send the [welcome guide](welcome-guide.md) the day the deposit lands. It sets
expectations while goodwill is highest — how feedback works, what you need
from them, when they'll see things.

Then write the [requirements doc](requirements-template.md) and get it signed
off with the [requirements sign-off form](requirements-feedback-form.md).

**This is the most valuable hour of the project.** Requirements are the thing
you point at every time scope drifts. Without them, "that's not what I asked
for" is unanswerable and you'll rebuild for free. With them, the same sentence
becomes "good idea — that's outside what we agreed, here's a change order."

Chase content from day one via the [content planner](content-planner.md) and
[asset checklist](asset-checklist.md).

---

## Stage 6 — Build

Head down. Show nothing until it's worth showing — a half-finished homepage
invites feedback on things you were about to fix anyway, and you can never
un-see a client's first reaction.

Send a Friday progress note either way. Silence makes clients anxious, and
anxious clients invent scope.

---

## Stage 7 — The two feedback rounds

### The revision trap

This is where studios lose money, so it's worth being precise about the
mechanism.

Unbounded revision doesn't fail because clients are unreasonable. It fails
because **feedback with no cost attached has no reason to converge.** If
round four is free, there's no moment where "good enough" becomes the rational
choice, and a client genuinely trying to help will keep helping forever.

Two rounds, written into the price and the contract, creates that moment.

### How it runs

**Round 1 — homepage only.** Direction, not detail. Use the
[homepage feedback form](homepage-feedback-form.md). You're testing whether
the look and structure are right; typos don't matter yet, and saying so out
loud saves everyone a wasted pass.

**Round 2 — the full site.** Use the
[website feedback form](website-feedback-form.md). This is polish and
correctness.

Rules, stated in the welcome guide and enforced kindly:

- One **consolidated** response per round, on the form, within 5 working days.
- Feedback arriving in dribs — texts, calls, a forwarded email from a cousin —
  gets collected politely and held until the round closes.
- Anything that isn't in the requirements is a change order, not feedback.
- A third round is a paid add-on at the rate-card price. Offer it cheerfully:
  "happy to do another pass — it's $[X], want me to add it?"

Ninety percent of clients never need round three. The ten percent who do are
the ones you'd otherwise have worked for free for.

---

## Stage 8 — Launch

Work the [launch checklist](launch-checklist.md). Never launch on a Friday.
Never launch the day before you travel.

Take a full backup of anything you're replacing *before* you point DNS. You
will need it roughly once every twenty projects, and on that day it's the
difference between an inconvenience and a catastrophe.

---

## Stage 9 — Handover and after

Send the [handover doc](handover-template.md) with final invoice. Transfer
credentials properly, revoke your own access to anything you shouldn't keep.

Pitch the [care plan](care-plan-agreement.md) at handover, when they're
happiest. Recurring revenue is what turns a studio from a treadmill into a
business — ten care plans at $250/mo is $30k a year that arrives whether or
not you sold anything that month.

Two weeks later, ask for the [testimonial](testimonial-request.md). Ask while
the result is fresh and specific.

---

## Money rules

- **Deposit before work.** Always.
- **Milestone payments on anything over six weeks.** Never carry more than a
  third of a project unpaid.
- **Final payment before launch, not after.** Leverage evaporates the moment
  the site is live.
- **Late fees exist to be mentioned, rarely to be charged.** Having the clause
  is what makes the polite reminder work.
- **Price the tier, not the hours.** Hourly punishes you for being fast.

---

## Things that will go wrong, and what to do

| What happens | What to do |
|---|---|
| Content never arrives | Written notice at 2 weeks. Pause the project and say so. Restart fee if it stretches past 30 days — the clause is in every contract. |
| "Can we just also…" | Warm yes, then a [change order](change-order.md). Every time. The first one you let slide sets the price for all of them. |
| A new stakeholder appears at round 2 | Their feedback is welcome and it's round 2's. If it contradicts signed requirements, it's a change order. Ask who has final say and get that in writing. |
| Client goes silent mid-build | Two emails, then a call, then a written pause notice. Don't keep building into a void. |
| They hate the first design | Return to the requirements and the branding questionnaire and find where the misread happened. Usually it's an unstated assumption. It's round 1 — this is what round 1 is for. |
| They want the source files / your Figma | That's a deliverable with a price, not an afterthought. Covered in the contracts. |
| Payment is late | The invoice reminder script in [email scripts](email-scripts.md). Friendly, specific, and references the clause. |

---

## Roles, if there are two of you

| Task | Who |
|---|---|
| Enquiry reply, call, proposal, contract | Lead / owner |
| Requirements doc | Lead, reviewed by whoever builds |
| Content and asset chasing | Whoever has the calmest email voice |
| Design, build | Builder |
| Round 1 & 2 collation | Lead — one voice to the client, always |
| Launch checklist | Builder, signed off by Lead |
| Handover, care plan pitch | Lead |

The rule that matters: **one voice to the client.** Two people replying to the
same client is how contradictory promises get made.
